rendered: The premise does not match the paper. It does not conclude that aqueous processing is incompatible with Ni-rich NMC. Its conclusion is the opposite: the paper states that aqueous processing is compatible with Ni-rich NMC 811[1]. The paper does acknowledge the lithium loss. It calls Li+/H+ exchange the main issue for water processing of NMC, and it notes that higher nickel content means more exchange. However, the measured leaching is small: even the most Ni-rich material shows only ~3 wt%[2] leached Li after one week[3]. XRD and Raman found no bulk structural changes, and XPS showed only minor surface changes. The pouch cells made with aqueous-processed NMC cathodes still still demonstrate very good electrochemical[4] performance. Their capacity retention is slightly lower than that of the NMP-processed cells (~70% vs. ~76%[5]), and the rate capability at higher discharge rates is 10–15% lower[6]. The authors attribute these gaps to the formulation, the cathode electrolyte interphase formed after water exposure, and possible transition-metal dissolution, and they say the formulation could be improved further. So the paper treats the lithium leaching as a challenge to manage, not as a reason to rule out aqueous processing.
